extracted.intended_audience: amateur aviators, hobbyist builders and experimenters wishing to construct and operate a 20-foot biplane glider (early-20th-century handbook audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Step-by-step practical handbook for constructing, trussing, covering, and safely operating a 20-foot biplane glider (Chanute-type) aimed at the amateur builder. Includes materials, dimensions, assembly, rigging, and flight guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of selected spruce for framework
rubrics_metrics.description: The framework is composed entirely of selected spruce, straight grained and free from knots.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spruce chosen because it is dense and tough yet light. Dimensions given are for finished, planed pieces. Round off corners to reduce air resistance. Finish wood by brushing with hot glue and water, rub down and coat with thin shellac; alternatively sand and use spar varnish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Horizontal beam dimensions and splicing
rubrics_metrics.description: Principal horizontal beams should measure 20 feet long, 1 1/2 inches wide and 3/4 inches thick (finished).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If 20-foot spruce is unavailable, splice two 10-foot pieces with a 5-foot splicing strip of same cross section tapered to 1/4 inch at ends; use six 3/16 inch round-headed stove bolts with washers; center spacing of bolts and washer placement specified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strut dimensions and notch/projection
rubrics_metrics.description: Horizontal struts: three feet long and 1/2 x 1 1/4 inches in cross section with a notch 1 1/2 x 3/4 inches cut in each end, forming a 1 1/2 x 1/2 x 1/2 inch projection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Struts fastened with one or two small wire nails and secured by a clamp. Positions: two center struts 2 feet apart, others 4 ft 6 in and 9 ft from center (see Fig. 3); upper-plane projections above horizontal members, lower-plane projections below.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strut clamps construction and placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Clamps are bent from sheet brass one sixteenth of an inch thick, 3 7/8 inches long and 1 inch wide with rounded ends and a 1/4 inch hole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clamps protect underside of beam from nut action and secure struts; two dozen required; bolts and washers pass through beams and clamps as illustrated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stanchion dimensions and sockets
rubrics_metrics.description: Stanchions: four feet long and 7/8 of an inch in diameter; sockets: base 3 1/4 inches long, 1 1/4 inches wide, 1/4 inch thick, cup internal diameter 7/8 inch, outside 1 1/4 inches, cup 1 inch high.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sockets preferably aluminum (light and strong) but brass or iron acceptable. Pattern should be slightly tapered for casting removal. Two dozen sockets required; two screws attach each socket to horizontal members; sockets permit ready disassembly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eyebolt specification and use
rubrics_metrics.description: Eyebolts: 1/4 inch stock, at least two inches long under the eye; eye diameter 1/2 inch. Four dozen required (two per socket).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eyebolts pass through sockets and beams, coming out under side opposite strut clamp; nuts under beam hold clamp tight. Eye bolts may be purchased threaded or blank and threaded by purchaser. Use washers under bolt heads and nuts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rib dimensions, spacing and fastening
rubrics_metrics.description: Ribs: 41 ribs, each 1/2 inch square in cross section and four feet long; fastened to horizontal members one foot apart, flush with front and projecting one foot at rear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use one or two small wire nails at front and a clamp screwed down with two No. 5 round-headed wood screws (1/2 inch long) at rear; pre-drill with brad awl to avoid splitting. Clamp dimensions: sheet copper strips 2 1/4 in long by 5/8 in wide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rib curvature and amount
rubrics_metrics.description: Surfaces are slightly curved: about four percent curve (approximately two inches for ribs four feet long).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steam ribs and bend to maintain curve when dry so they will not push horizontal beams apart. Provide same small curvature for all ribs. Avoid flat planes relying on air pressure to create curve (inefficient). Some claim parabolic curve best—author doubts it; Wright curve close to arc of circle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigid ribs and strongly trussed frame
rubrics_metrics.description: Ribs must be perfectly rigid and the whole frame strongly trussed so it cannot be distorted by air pressure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Smithsonian/Langley experiments: lack of rigidity caused moments of distortion that wrecked flights. Make sustaining surfaces rigid to avoid bending under pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arm piece dimensions and placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Arm pieces: two strips of wood 3 feet long, 1 inch wide and 1 3/4 inches deep, fastened to horizontal beams with 3/16 inch round-headed stove bolts; distance between approx. 13 inches for average person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Upper side of arm pieces rounded; do not pad with cloth (impedes movement and balance). Adjust spacing for operator breadth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rudder construction and non-movability
rubrics_metrics.description: Rudder composed of two planes at right angles (vertical and horizontal) in rear of main surfaces; neither rudder plane is movable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vertical portion keeps machine headed into wind; horizontal steadies longitudinally and prevents pitching. Rudder framework sticks cross-section one inch square; long beams A are 8 ft 11 in; uprights B 3 ft 10 in; horizontal strips include C (6 ft) and D (2 ft). Rudder is detachable via sockets on body.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rudder beam sockets and alignment
rubrics_metrics.description: Rudder beams step into sockets on the machine; sockets must be perfectly aligned on a line at right angles to horizontal members through plane center.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two sockets per plane (small and large brass variants) with 3/16 inch holes for stove bolts. A bolt through the top of the small socket prevents beam pulling out. Four 3/16 inch bolts near plane corners accept piano wires for bracing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Covering material and quantity
rubrics_metrics.description: Surfaces formed of cambric or muslin; thirty yards of material one yard wide sufficient to cover machine including rudders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Motor-driven aeroplanes may use rubberized silk or 'continental' balloon cloth; varnishing suggested to improve efficiency but expensive. One gallon of aero varnish covers ~100 sq ft depending on weave.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cloth strip layout and reinforcing over ribs
rubrics_metrics.description: Cut seven strips 4 ft 6 1/2 in long and sew along selvages to make a surface 4 ft 6 1/2 in wide and a little over 20 ft long; sew 21 strips 4 ft 6 1/2 in by 1 1/2 in at right angles across surface one foot apart (center lines).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Edges of these strips turned under 1/4 in on each side to form 1-inch reinforcement that will be directly above each rib.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long edge hemming and reinforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Long edges doubled and hemmed: turn under 1/4 inch forming a 3-inch hem, then double back one inch and sew again yielding a two-inch hem of two (back from edge four thicknesses at one inch).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reinforcement prevents ripping/tearing under tack heads when under flight pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bottom-plane cloth layout
rubrics_metrics.description: Bottom planes made of two sections divided by center opening for operator; sections are reinforced same as top plane but one foot less than half as long.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Space in center left for body of operator; reinforce edges similarly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tacking cloth and protecting ribs
rubrics_metrics.description: Cloth tacked over front horizontal beam, stretched tightly over curved ribs and fastened with tacks; tacks along ribs spaced about 4 inches apart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use brass-headed upholsterer's nails not long enough to pass through ribs; place felt strip 3/8 in wide and 4 ft long over each rib between tack head and cloth to reduce tearing. Use heavy weight under rib while tacking. Alternative: sew pocket on underside to slip ribs into.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rudder covering
rubrics_metrics.description: Rudder planes covered on both sides with fabric stretched tightly and tacked along edges; edges turned under before tacking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Edges of plane cloth should be securely fastened to struts by tacks to relieve ribs of strain and prevent pulling toward center.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trussing strength requirement (load test)
rubrics_metrics.description: When tightened, piano-wire trussing should brace the framework so it will support without appreciable sag or strain a heavy man hanging from the arm pieces and the ends of the planes resting on carpenters' horses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a practical test for sufficient truss tension and overall rigidity before flight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trussing method 1 (diagonal wires, no turnbuckles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Method 1: each wire fastened to an eyebolt on horizontal beam then run diagonally across to the socket on opposite beam; four diagonal wires brace each large cell; middle cell braced by wires across diagonals of its rectangles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simpler, no turnbuckles required, and adequate for ordinary glider. Anchor wires as illustrated and adjust tension with nuts on lower eye bolts. Use anchoring method with short copper tubing and bent hook on wire end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trussing method 2 (turnbuckles in diagonals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Method 2: include a turnbuckle in the diagonal of every rectangle except those formed by stanchions with horizontal beams; this is used on almost all aeroplanes and is considered strongest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stronger but harder to true up (tightening one diagonal requires loosening the other). Recommended for those willing to accept extra expense and labor. Turnbuckles also required on rudder bracing wires.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anchoring piano wires
rubrics_metrics.description: Anchor piano wire by passing it through a short piece of 1/8 inch copper tubing (~3/8 inch long), then through eyebolt, double back through tube, bend extreme end into hook and shove tube close to eyebolt so wire cannot pull out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pull wire tight before bending final hook; regulate tension afterward by turning nuts on lower ends of eye bolts or via turnbuckles where included.

rubrics_metrics.name: Turnbuckle construction (bicycle spoke nipple)
rubrics_metrics.description: Turnbuckles made from bicycle spoke and nipple: cut spoke to use threaded part, bend end into an eye; sheet brass and sheet iron pieces form body; spoke nipple admitted into brass piece and prevented from passing all the way by shoulder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Piano wire passes through rounded strap ends; tension regulated by turning spoke nipple while holding spoke rigid. Inexpensive and simple to make.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frame truing and alignment
rubrics_metrics.description: After fastening wires, the frame must be perfectly true and not warped or twisted; especially the rudder must be true with rest of machine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: True up by sighting along horizontal beams and tightening/loosening specific wires to correct any curvature or twist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disassembly procedure for storage
rubrics_metrics.description: To take the glider apart remove bolts holding rudder beams, unfasten or loosen truss wires/turnbuckles, remove eyebolts from sockets, then remove stanchions and lay planes one atop the other for compact storage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designed to be 'knocked down' and stored in cellar/under porch; sockets and eyebolts facilitate disassembly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational safety: wind and site limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not attempt gliding over ground broken by trees or when wind blowing over 12–15 miles per hour; avoid starting from precipitous cliffs or buildings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eddy currents around objects cause unpredictable rising/falling currents; begin by running against wind on level ground making short jumps, then progress to gentle slopes. Otto Lilienthal cautioned against high/cliff starts due to rebounding gusts and suspension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational caution and phased practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Emphasize caution and methodical progression: start on level ground, make short jumps, practice until competent before transferring to slopes and increasing glide length.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cautions not meant to imply extreme danger but to recommend judgment, not impatience. Wright brothers practiced methodically for years before powered flight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understanding airflow and lift
rubrics_metrics.description: Front edge elevation creates an angle so air follows curve and leaves rear downward, producing upward reaction/ lift; center of pressure lies somewhat forward of geometric center due to curvature and front-edge disturbance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Knowledge of rising/falling eddies and effects of obstacles is crucial to site selection and flight control; illustrations and analogies (skater on thin ice) provided to explain lift concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equilibrium and center-of-gravity control
rubrics_metrics.description: Glider remains in equilibrium only while center of gravity of machine+operator falls in same vertical line as pressure exerted by air; forward CG causes nose-down, rear CG nose-up, lateral CG offset causes roll.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pilot controls equilibrium in flight by moving legs and body; shifting CG forward by swinging legs/body causes descent; moving backward induces rise—used in landing technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balancing and in-flight control by body movement
rubrics_metrics.description: Balance during flight accomplished by moving legs and body toward the side which is highest; shift CG forward/back to control pitch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For landing, push body toward back so glider tips up slightly, loses momentum and settles slowly onto feet. Don't pad arm pieces which would impede movements needed for balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost and economic expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Raw material cost if owner builds: usually a little less than $20 and should not exceed $35; a finished glider worth $50 to $100 depending on quantity built.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimate excludes optional varnishing. Affordability is emphasized as reason the amateur should attempt construction himself.
